description_full: Rockwell Automation, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, provides industrial automation and digital transformation solutions in North America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, the Asia Pacific, and Latin America. It operates in three segments: Intelligent Devices, Software & Control, and Lifecycle Services. The company offers drives, motion, material handling, safety, sensing, industrial components, hardware, software, and configured-to-order products; and control and visualization software and hardware, digital twin, simulation and information software, network and security infrastructure, and custom-engineered systems and software. It also provides digital consulting services; professional services, including engineered-to-order solutions; recurring services, such as cybersecurity, safety, asset management, and remote monitoring; customer technical support and repair services; optimization consulting services; and training services, as well as spare parts. The company sells its products through independent distributors in relation to its direct sales force. It serves discrete end markets, including automotive, semiconductor, e-commerce, and warehouse automation; hybrid end markets, such as food and beverage, household and personal care, and life sciences; and process end markets, including energy, mining, and chemicals. The company was formerly known as Rockwell International Corporation and changed its name to Rockwell Automation, Inc. in February 2002. Rockwell Automation, Inc. was incorporated in 1996 and is headquartered in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

financial_summary: Rockwell Automation, Inc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $44.8B market cap on $9.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -0% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 21% against a 10% cost of capital — a 12-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 41%.

The business throws off $1.7B in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.39× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.3× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 14× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 4.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
